Personally, my favorite is The Name of the Wind by Patrick Rothfuss. It draws you in immediately and, unbeknownst to the reader, casually drops threads on your heart throughout the book. The Silmarillion, above all others. I'm an aspiring Fantasy writer, and I read a lot. There are books I have enjoyed more than the Silmarillion, and books I have enjoyed in different ways, but I keep going back to Tolkien.

I'll try to explain. I myself have only the one Fantasy world in my head, and it's been there since I was 12, always growing, sometimes changing. I have only the one story line I want to write about (and have written about 95% of the first book), in addition to the world history. LotR was very enjoyable to me, but it's very clear when reading it that, despite being the longest story told about that world, the world and its history is so much larger than the reader sees. And that's how I feel about my own project - I love my world, and in Tolkien I find someone who seems to have felt the same about his own creation as I do about mine. I do wish he had been able to put the Silmarillion together himself, of course, but even edited by his son, the Silmarillion means a lot to me.
I hope to read your books some day!

One Hundred Years of Solitude by Gabriel Garcia Marquez.

A pretty popular choice for favourite book, no doubt. Were you expecting something more unusual, or something deliciously obscure? Sorry to disappoint, but there's a reason why so many people cite it as their favourite book.

I first read this while teaching English abroad; there was a public holiday and so I went looking for something to read over my four days off. As it turned out - I didn't pick it up for the first 2 days, which was a mistake because once I started in, withing the first few pages I was mesmerised. This was my first introduction to magical realism, and he paints such a vivid picture of Macondo, its confusing inhabitants and their intertwined stories and lives that it just pulled me in.

I spent almost every waking hour reading it over the next two days which is a shame because it deserves a much more careful approach. I just managed to finish reading with barely any time to spare before going back to work. It left my mind in a spin and I've been back to re-read it several times since to really appreciate everything it offers.

I loved the prose and the confusing array of characters and the machinations of a family's course through history with their inevitable mix of human and supernatural events all set to a backdrop that can't possible exist and yet it seems so natural and believable that you don't even question it.

Magnificent.

I always thought this was such a hard question. I tend toward sci fi, and there are so many great books there. Moon Is a Harsh Mistress, Man In The High Castle, Dune, Foundation, many others. But there's also, Temple Of My Familiar by Alice Walker and The works of Douglas Coupland, Tom Robbins, Walker Percy, and whomever pops in to my head immediately after I post this. All of that runs through my head, and then I think, oh yeah. Forget those. The Hitchiker's Guide To The Galaxy wins hands down. I read these books much too young, and kept reading them each year until I got all the jokes. They were formative to who I am. I've re-read them more than any other book. (I have a hard bound collection and I'm considering the entire series as one book). The fact that the characters are so disinterested in following the plot they end up following, to me make the books more than the mere farce that many people may find them to be. They seem more interested in finding something witty to say rather than saving the day or anything. I can relate to the characters completely. Plus, when Dent Arthur Dent learns to fly, he gets hit in the back by a large and unruly party. I really need to go ahead and read it again. Don't Panic!

Mine is "The Time Machine" by H. G. Wells.

Years and years ago, I read the story and thoroughly enjoyed it for what it was. It wasn't until fairly recently that I discovered that the Time Machine was actually an early example of the Dying-Earth sub-genre of post- apocalyptic science-fiction.

A genre that has always interested me, as evidenced by my first ever written story that had gratuitous amounts of the post-apocalyptic scenery, which I wrote as part of a grade-school project. Talk about a heavy-handed subject for a such a young mind!

Thanks to that books and that discovery, a part of me now fancies the thought that I could, at some point, become the author most prominently known for expanding and popularizing the Dying Earth sub-genre. But that's a just a pipe dream considering I generally don't release my works to the public.

With that said; I have many other favorites but at the risk of running off on a tangent, I choose to keep them.. Nameless ;-)
